h1: The 6 Best NAS for Small Businesses of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best NAS for Small Businesses: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: six NAS units for small businesses, from 2-bay starters to 4-bay Synology and UGREEN models, with software and RAID notes.
summary: The Synology DS925+ is the best NAS for small businesses, with four bays, DSM software, directory sync and Plus-tier support eligibility. The UGREEN DXP4800 Plus offers four bays and a five core Pentium Gold for less. The DS725+ is the expandable two-bay starter, the QNAP TS-264 ships with 8GB of RAM, and the DXP2800 and DS423 are the budget entries.
intro: Small businesses tend to get a NAS wrong at the bay count. Two bays feel generous on day one, but a mirrored pair gives you the capacity of a single drive, and the first time the team outgrows it you are migrating data in the middle of a deadline. Redundancy and growth room cost far less to buy at the start than to retrofit.

We reviewed eight NAS enclosures aimed at small teams and ranked six, scoring them on the Primea framework with bay count, RAID support, software, processor and memory, and business support weighted most. Every unit is diskless, so drive costs sit on top of the price bucket, and none of these replaces an offsite backup. Think about who maintains it, as much as what it costs.

products.name: Synology 4-Bay DiskStation DS925+ (Diskless)
products.verdict: Four bays, mature software and the most room to grow.
products.description:
The DS925+ is a four-bay diskless NAS running Synology DSM, with directory sync support and multi-bay RAID for redundancy. It is a Plus-tier model eligible for business support and can be expanded as storage needs grow, in the $500 and up bucket. Directory sync lets staff log in with existing company credentials, which cuts account chores.

It ranks first because it combines headroom with the most mature software in this group. The UGREEN beats it on raw processor per dollar, but not on ecosystem or support options.

Buy it for a growing team that needs room, support and a stable platform. The caveats are that drives are sold separately and it sits in the highest price bucket, so skip it if budget matters more than ecosystem.
products.idealFor: Growing teams that need room and support.

products.name: UGREEN NAS DXP4800 Plus 4-Bay NAS
products.verdict: Four bays and a five core Pentium Gold for less than Synology.
products.description:
The DXP4800 Plus is a four-bay diskless NAS with an Intel Pentium Gold 8505 five core CPU, RAID across all bays and cloud backup integration. UGREEN positions it at a value tier against premium four-bay rivals, in the $500 and up bucket. A five-core processor helps when several users hit shared files and run apps at once.

It ranks second because it matches the DS925+ on bay count while offering a stronger listed processor for less money. What it lacks is the track record: UGREEN's software ecosystem is younger than Synology's.

Buy it if you want strong CPU power on a tighter budget. The caveat is the newer software and no included drives, so skip it if your team relies on Synology tools or wants the established support path.
products.idealFor: Teams wanting strong CPU on a tighter budget.

products.name: Synology DS725+ Expandable NAS Storage (2-Bay, Diskless)
products.verdict: Start with two bays and expand without replacing it.
products.description:
The DS725+ is a two-bay diskless NAS that can be expanded, with Plus-tier support eligibility, private cloud storage and directory sync through DSM, in the $500 and up bucket. An expansion path means you add capacity later without replacing the unit, which spares you a migration.

It ranks third because two bays limit redundancy to a mirrored pair, while the DS925+ offers more headroom. Against the DXP4800 Plus, it trades processing power for the Synology ecosystem and a proper growth route.

Buy it for a small office planning to expand later. The caveats are only two bays and a premium price for the capacity. Skip it if you already need four bays, because you would pay for a unit you outgrow.
products.idealFor: Small offices planning to expand later.

products.name: QNAP TS-264-8G-US 2-Bay Desktop NAS
products.verdict: A two bay desktop NAS with 8GB RAM already installed.
products.description:
The QNAP TS-264 is a two-bay desktop NAS with 8GB of RAM included, running QNAP QTS software with directory sync and cloud backup support, in the $200 to $500 bucket. Memory matters when a NAS runs several apps and serves many users, and 8GB already installed saves an upgrade.

It ranks fourth because it lacks the expandability emphasis of the DS725+, but it includes more memory out of the box and costs a bucket less. It also gives you a choice outside Synology.

Buy it if your team prefers QNAP's ecosystem or you want memory included. The caveats are two bays only and a QTS learning curve. Skip it if you want Synology DSM, since the interface and app library differ.

products.name: UGREEN NAS DXP2800 2-Bay
products.verdict: An entry-level two bay unit with RAID 1 mirroring.
products.description:
The DXP2800 is a two-bay diskless NAS aimed at creators and small teams, with gigabit networking and RAID 1 mirroring at an entry price, in the $200 to $500 bucket. RAID 1 keeps a full copy on a second drive, so one drive can fail without losing files.

It ranks fifth because gigabit networking is standard rather than fast and it offers fewer growth options. Against the TS-264, it costs about the same but lacks listed memory and a stated software ecosystem advantage.

Buy it for a solo business centralizing files. The caveats are the gigabit limit and limited growth. Skip it if you expect to outgrow two bays, because there is no listed expansion path.
products.skipIf: You expect to outgrow two bays.

products.name: Synology DS423 Family & Business Backup (4-Bay, Diskless)
products.verdict: A value-tier four bay for backup and surveillance.
products.description:
The DS423 is a four-bay diskless value-tier Synology with support for video surveillance storage, a photo vault and secure file sharing, in the $200 to $500 bucket. Four bays at that price is the draw, and Surveillance Station support suits an office with cameras.

It ranks last because it is a value model with fewer team features than the Plus-tier DS925+. It undercuts the DS925+ by a bucket but lacks the business support eligibility and the expansion headroom.

Buy it for an office combining backup and cameras. The caveat is the value-tier tooling, so skip it if you want Plus-tier business support, and plan to budget for the drives on top.

whatMatters.detail: Each bay holds one drive. A mirrored pair gives you the space of one drive, while four bays allow parity setups with more usable space. Count the bays and decide what RAID level you want, then plan the total capacity you need in two years, not today, since adding bays later usually means replacing the unit. Drive prices fall, but migrations never get cheaper.

RAID spreads or copies data across drives so one failure does not lose files. RAID 1 mirrors two drives, and larger arrays use parity. Check the listing for supported RAID types, and remember RAID is not a backup. A deleted file or a fire takes everything, so keep an offsite copy. A second NAS or cloud copy closes the gap.

The software decides how easy it is to set up users, shares and backups. Synology DSM, QNAP QTS and UGREEN's system differ in polish and app support. Read what features the listing names, such as directory sync and cloud backup, and ask which ecosystem your IT contact already knows. Support time is the hidden cost.

The processor and memory affect how well the NAS handles several users and apps at once. A listed CPU model and RAM figure are good signs. Look for them in the bullets, as with the DXP4800 Plus's Pentium Gold or the TS-264's 8GB, and be wary when neither is stated. Weak memory shows up the moment two people sync large folders.

Diskless means no drives are included, so the real cost is the enclosure plus the drives. Use drives rated for NAS use, which are built for continuous operation. Budget for them on top of the enclosure, and buy a matching set so a failed drive can be replaced with an identical one. Mixed batches complicate recovery.

faq.q: Do these NAS units include hard drives?
faq.a: No. The Synology, QNAP and UGREEN models listed here are diskless, so you buy drives separately and should budget for them on top of the price bucket, because drives often cost as much as the enclosure.

faq.q: Is RAID the same as a backup?
faq.a: No. RAID protects against a drive failure but not deletion, ransomware or fire. Keep a separate backup copy, even on a four-bay unit like the DS925+. A second location is the real safety net.

Use NAS-rated drives built for continuous operation. Check the maker's compatibility list for the model you choose, since Synology and UGREEN publish their own lists. Mixed brands in one array make recovery harder.

For a small team, yes. A mirrored pair gives one drive of usable space, so plan capacity accordingly. The DS725+ lets you expand later, while the DXP2800 does not list an expansion path. Mirrored capacity runs out sooner than people expect.

faq.q: How do I connect staff to the NAS?
faq.a: Join it to your network, create user accounts and set shared folders. Directory sync, which the DS925+ and TS-264 list, helps if you use a central login for staff, since it removes duplicate passwords.

faq.q: Can I move drives to a new NAS later?
faq.a: Often within the same brand, but check compatibility. Back up first, and read the maker's migration guide before moving drives between a DS423 and a DS925+, because layouts and firmware must match.

finalTake: Pick the DS925+ for a team that expects to grow and wants mature software and support. The DXP4800 Plus is the choice when processor power per dollar matters most, and the DS725+ or TS-264 suits smaller offices. The DXP2800 and DS423 keep costs low. Budget for drives separately, and keep a second copy of important files somewhere else.
